rows.stem: In its extended 'beads-on-string' form of chromatin, the 'beads' are composed of :

options.label: B
options.text: Histones and about 200 bp of DNA

options.label: D
options.text: NHC proteins and about 200 bp of DNA

rows.solution: In the nucleus the negatively charged DNA is wrapped around a positively charged **histone octamer** (eight histone molecules), forming a unit called the **nucleosome**. A typical nucleosome contains about **200 bp of DNA** helix. Repeating nucleosomes form the chromatin thread, which under the electron microscope looks like **beads on a string**: each bead is a nucleosome (histones plus about 200 bp of DNA), and the **linker DNA** joining them is the string, not part of the bead. The non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins are needed only for packing chromatin at a higher level. So the answer is option (B) Histones and about 200 bp of DNA.

rows.stem:
Given below are few statements with respect to the process of oogenesis in a human ovary :
(i) Each granulosa cell gets surrounded by a primary oocyte to form the primary follicle.
(ii) A couple of million of oogonia are formed within each fetal ovary during the embryonic development.
(iii) Tertiary follicle is characterised by antrum and theca layers.
(iv) Secondary follicles form a zona pellucida layer around it.
(v) Mature graafian follicle ruptures to release the secondary oocyte from the ovary.
Choose the option with all true statements from the given options :
rows.solution:
Checking each statement against the stages of oogenesis:
- (i) is false: it is the other way round. Each **primary oocyte** gets surrounded by a layer of **granulosa cells** to form the primary follicle.
- (ii) is true: oogenesis starts during embryonic development, when a couple of million gamete mother cells (**oogonia**) are formed within each fetal ovary.
- (iii) is true: the **tertiary follicle** is characterised by a fluid-filled cavity called the **antrum**, and its theca layer is organised into an inner theca interna and an outer theca externa.
- (iv) is false: the secondary follicle only gains more layers of granulosa cells and a new theca. The **zona pellucida** is formed later by the **secondary oocyte** inside the Graafian follicle, as a new membrane around itself.
- (v) is true: the mature Graafian follicle ruptures to release the secondary oocyte (ovum) from the ovary, which is **ovulation**.

So the true statements are (ii), (iii) and (v). So the answer is option (B) (ii), (iii), (v).

rows.stem: The simplest definition of a gene in eukaryotes is – A unit of DNA that has information to mainly specify the synthesis of :

options.label: A
options.text: Single polypeptide chain and mRNA only

options.label: B
options.text: Many polypeptide chains and mRNA only

options.label: C
options.text: Single polypeptide chain and functional RNA only

options.label: D
options.text: Many polypeptide chains and functional RNA only

rows.solution:
In eukaryotes the structural genes are **monocistronic**: one gene (cistron) carries the information for **one polypeptide chain**. Some genes are never translated at all; their final product is a **functional RNA** such as tRNA or rRNA, which works as RNA itself. So the simplest working definition of a gene is a unit of DNA that specifies either a single polypeptide or a functional RNA.
- "Many polypeptide chains" describes a polycistronic unit, which is typical of bacteria, not of eukaryotic genes.
- "mRNA only" is too narrow: mRNA is only the intermediate for a polypeptide, and it leaves out the genes whose end product is tRNA or rRNA.

So the answer is option (C) Single polypeptide chain and functional RNA only.

rows.stem: A colourblind man marries a woman with normal sight who has no history of colourblindness in her family. What is the probability of their son being colourblind ?
rows.solution:
Colour blindness is a **sex-linked recessive** trait carried on the X chromosome.
- The colourblind man is \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\text{Y}\).
- The woman has normal sight and no family history, so she is homozygous normal, \(\text{X}\text{X}\).

A son always receives his **X chromosome from the mother** and his Y chromosome from the father. Every son of this couple gets a normal X from the mother and the Y from the father, so every son is \(\text{X}\text{Y}\), normal. The father's \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\) goes only to his daughters, who will all be carriers \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\text{X}\) with normal vision. The probability of a colourblind son is therefore zero. So the answer is option (C) Nil.

rows.stem: The type of antibodies produced during an immune response to allergens as dust and pollen grains in a person is :
rows.solution: An **allergy** is the exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens present in the environment, called **allergens**, such as dust, pollen grains and mites. The antibodies produced in response to them are of the **IgE type**. These cause the release of chemicals like **histamine and serotonin** from mast cells, producing sneezing, watery eyes, a running nose and difficulty in breathing. So the answer is option (A) IgE.

rows.stem:
Select the statements that are true for a typical megasporangium of flowering plants.
(i) It is attached to the placenta by hilum.
(ii) It has a chalaza end that represents the basal part of the ovule.
(iii) It has nucellus enclosed by integuments.
(iv) Its micropylar end is known as chalaza.
Choose the correct answer :
rows.solution:
The megasporangium is the **ovule**.
- (i) is false: the ovule is attached to the placenta by a stalk called the **funicle**. The **hilum** is only the region where the body of the ovule fuses with the funicle.
- (ii) is true: opposite the micropylar end lies the **chalaza**, which represents the basal part of the ovule.
- (iii) is true: the body of the ovule is a mass of cells, the **nucellus**, enclosed by one or two protective envelopes, the **integuments**.
- (iv) is false: the micropylar end carries the **micropyle**, the small opening left by the integuments at the tip; the chalaza is the end opposite to it.

So the true statements are (ii) and (iii). So the answer is option (B) (ii) and (iii).

rows.stem: The primates that probably lived in East Africa grasslands about two mya were :
rows.solution: About **2 mya**, the man-like primates called **Australopithecines** probably lived in the East African grasslands. Evidence shows that they hunted with stone weapons but essentially ate fruit. Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus are much older, existing about 15 mya, while the Neanderthal man lived in east and central Asian countries between 1,00,000 and 40,000 years back. So the answer is option (C) Australopithecines.

rows.stem:
Use the given information to select the amino acid attached to the 3' end of tRNA during the process of translation, if the coding strand of the structural gene being transcribed has the nucleotide sequence 'ATA'.
Codons for the amino acids :
UAU – Tyrosine
AUG – Methionine
AUA – Isoleucine
AGU – Serine
rows.solution:
The mRNA has the same sequence as the **coding strand** of the gene, with uracil in place of thymine.
- Coding strand: ATA, so the mRNA codon is **AUA**.
- From the given codons, AUA codes for **isoleucine**.

During translation the tRNA whose anticodon (UAU) pairs with the codon AUA carries isoleucine attached at its 3' end. (Reading the codon as UAU, the complement of ATA, would wrongly give tyrosine; that complement is the anticodon on the tRNA, not the codon.) So the answer is option (A) Isoleucine.

rows.stem: Early detection of HIV in suspected AIDS patients can be done using the diagnostic technique of :
rows.solution: **PCR** (Polymerase Chain Reaction) amplifies even a very low amount of nucleic acid of a pathogen many times, so the infection can be detected while the patient shows no symptoms and the pathogen is still present in very small numbers. For this reason PCR is now routinely used to detect **HIV in suspected AIDS patients**. Antibody-based tests such as ELISA depend on the antigens or antibodies building up to a detectable level, so they come later. RNAi is a method of silencing genes used for pest resistance, and ESTs are expressed sequence tags used in genome sequencing. So the answer is option (B) PCR.

rows.stem: Large holes in 'Swiss cheese' are formed by the activity of microbes :
rows.solution: The large holes in **Swiss cheese** are due to the production of a large amount of **carbon dioxide** by the bacterium **Propionibacterium shermanii** (printed here as 'sharmanii'). The other microbes do different jobs: Streptococcus pneumoniae causes pneumonia, Monascus purpureus yields the blood-cholesterol lowering statins, and Trichoderma polysporum produces the immunosuppressant cyclosporin A. So the answer is option (D) Propionibacterium sharmanii.

rows.stem: In pea plant (Pisum sativum) axial flower position is dominant over terminal flower position. The expected ratio of phenotypes of the offspring in a cross between both the parents with heterozygous axial flower will be :
rows.solution:
Let F stand for the dominant allele for axial flower position and f for the recessive allele for terminal position. Both parents are heterozygous axial, \(\text{Ff}\).
- Each parent forms two kinds of gametes, F and f, in equal numbers.
- \(\text{Ff} \times \text{Ff}\) gives the genotypes \(\text{FF} : \text{Ff} : \text{ff} = 1 : 2 : 1\).
- FF and Ff both show axial flowers, because F is dominant; only ff shows terminal flowers.

The phenotypic ratio is therefore axial : terminal = 3 : 1, Mendel's monohybrid ratio. So the answer is option (A) 3 : 1.

rows.stem: Write two features of an ideal contraceptive. Explain any one natural contraceptive method that makes the chances of conception almost nil.
rows.solution:
**Features of an ideal contraceptive** (any two):
- It should be **user-friendly** and **easily available**.
- It should be **effective** and **reversible**, with **no or least side effects**.
- It should in no way interfere with the sexual drive, desire and/or the sexual act of the user.

**A natural method: lactational amenorrhea.** Lactational amenorrhea means the absence of menstruation. It is based on the fact that **ovulation, and therefore the menstrual cycle, does not occur during the period of intense lactation** following parturition. So as long as the mother breast-feeds the child fully, the **chances of conception are almost nil**. The method has been reported to be effective only up to a maximum of **six months** after parturition.

The marking scheme also accepts the other natural methods: **periodic abstinence**, in which the couple avoid coitus from day 10 to 17 of the menstrual cycle, when ovulation is expected; and **withdrawal (coitus interruptus)**, in which the male partner withdraws his penis from the vagina just before ejaculation.

Both are assisted reproductive technologies used to help infertile couples.
- **GIFT (Gamete Intra Fallopian Transfer):** an **ovum collected from a donor** is transferred into the **fallopian tube** of another female who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and further development. Fertilisation then takes place inside her body.
- **ICSI (Intra Cytoplasmic Sperm Injection):** a specialised procedure to form an embryo in the laboratory, in which a **sperm is directly injected into the ovum** in vitro. The embryo so formed is then transferred into the female.

rows.stem:
Thomas Hunt Morgan carried out several dihybrid crosses in Drosophila melanogaster to study genes that were sex linked.
(a) Give four major reasons for using the tiny fruit flies by Morgan for his experiments.
(b) How did Morgan and his group explain the physical association of the two genes on a chromosome to the frequency of recombination between gene pairs on the same chromosome ?
rows.solution:
(a) **Reasons for choosing Drosophila melanogaster** (any four):
- The flies could be **grown on a simple synthetic medium** in the laboratory.
- They **complete their life cycle in about two weeks**, so many generations can be studied quickly.
- A **single mating produces a large number of progeny** flies.
- There is a **clear differentiation of the sexes**: the male and female flies are easily distinguishable.
- They show **many types of hereditary variations**, which can be seen easily with a low power microscope.

(b) Morgan found that when two genes were on the same chromosome, the parental gene combinations appeared in the progeny far more often than the non-parental (recombinant) ones. He called the physical association of genes on a chromosome **linkage**, and the generation of non-parental gene combinations **recombination**. He explained the link between them through how strongly the genes are linked:
- **Tightly linked genes** (lying close together) show **very low recombination frequency**.
- **Loosely linked genes** (lying farther apart) show **higher recombination frequency**.

For example, the genes for white eye and yellow body showed only 1.3 per cent recombination, while white eye and miniature wing showed 37.2 per cent. Morgan's student Alfred Sturtevant later used the frequency of recombination between gene pairs on the same chromosome as a measure of the distance between them and mapped their positions on the chromosome.

rows.stem:
(i) Name the two genes encoding for the Bt toxin protein used in biotechnology for the control of cotton bollworms.
(ii) How does the expression of Bt toxin gene in Bt cotton plant help in providing resistance to cotton bollworms ? Explain.
rows.solution:
(i) The two genes are **cryIAc** and **cryIIAb**; the proteins they encode control the cotton bollworms. (cryIAb is the gene that controls the corn borer.)

(ii) The gene comes from the soil bacterium **Bacillus thuringiensis** (Bt). Inserting it into cotton makes the plant itself produce the toxin, so it resists bollworms without insecticide sprays. The toxin works as follows:
- The **cry** gene codes for a toxic insecticidal protein that forms **protein crystals** during expression.
- The protein is present in an **inactive protoxin** form, so it does not harm the plant (or the bacterium) that makes it.
- When a bollworm feeds on the cotton plant, it ingests the inactive toxin.
- The **alkaline pH of the insect's gut** solubilises the crystals and converts the protoxin into the **active toxin**.
- The activated toxin **binds to the surface of the midgut epithelial cells**.
- It **creates pores** in these cells, which causes **cell swelling and lysis**.
- The gut is destroyed and the bollworm **eventually dies**.

So the plant carries its own pesticide, made in an inactive form and switched on only inside the insect's gut.

rows.stem:
(i) Explain the given methods of introducing the alien DNA in the host cells :
(I) Biolistics
(II) Microinjection
(ii) How is E. coli made 'competent' to take up a recombinant plasmid or DNA ?
rows.solution:
(i)
(I) **Biolistics (gene gun):** the cells are bombarded with **high velocity micro-particles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA**. The particles pierce the cells and carry the alien DNA in. This method is suitable mainly for **plant cells**.

(II) **Microinjection:** the recombinant DNA is **injected directly into the nucleus of an animal cell** using a fine micro-needle.

(ii) DNA is a hydrophilic molecule and cannot pass through cell membranes, so the bacterial cells must first be made **competent** to take it up:
- The E. coli cells are treated with a **specific concentration of a divalent cation, such as calcium**. This increases the efficiency with which DNA enters the bacterium through (temporary) **pores in its cell wall**.
- The cells are then incubated with the recombinant DNA **on ice**, given a brief **heat shock at \(42^{\circ}\text{C}\)**, and placed back on ice.

This lets the bacterial cells take up the recombinant plasmid or DNA.
